segments: And he used to cover his face with a veil,
and he showed that he was zealous for the law that had been trodden down.
And he too began to loot
and to kill.
And he went up to Jerusalem and wanted to burn the churches,
but much gold was given to him by the patriarch, and he departed.
And Raja the commander came against him,
and killed eight thousand of his men.
And they captured a thousand [men] and Abu Harb himself while he was swallowed up [in hiding],
and sent them to al-Mu'tasim.
And at this time, Musa the chief of the Kurds rebelled in the land of Qardu.
And the Persians came against him in the winter season,
and the Kurds destroyed about fourteen {OCR?: ܝܲܡܥܲܥܤܲܪ} thousand of the Persians,
because the rebels would come out from their dwellings well-rested,
while the Persians were numb with cold and their fingers were falling off.
And at that time there was a severe famine and a harsh pestilence, and distress from the heavy burden of exactions and from the rebels.
For the Daraeans, the Nisibisans, and the Amidans went out in rebellion,
and the Persians came against them and destroyed them.
And because they were not killing Christians,
many Arabs were saved by the sign of the cross.
And in the year 1154
(1154 of the Greeks,
843 of our Lord?), al-Mu'tasim died.
And at his death he freed eight thousand silver-bought slaves.
And he also left forty thousand horses for riding,
and twenty thousand mules for baggage,
and thirty thousand stable slaves.
And in those days Theophilos the king of the Romans also died.
After al-Mu'tasim, his son al-Wathiq [reigned] five years and nine months.
This [caliph] oppressed
the scribes (nomikoi) of his realm with severe tortures,
and took from them many tens of thousands of dinars.
And in the year that al-Wathiq became king,
which was the year 1155,
over the Romans,
being a child three years old.
And his mother Theodora was administering the kingdom,
while Manuel was appointed commander-in-chief over all the troops.
And the Romans sent an ambassador to the Arabs concerning the matter of peace
and concerning the exchange of captives.
And when the ambassador of the Romans arrived,
al-Wathiq, the king of the Arabs, received him joyfully.
And he did not speak arrogant words like his father, who had said:
"We do not agree that the Christians should be equal in number to the Arabs in the exchange."
notes: 1155 of the Greeks (844 of our Lord?): Michael, the son of Theophilos, also became king
